Part 1: https://youtu.be/2rSEP3gmDR0
--------
Former DEA agent Chris Feistl sits down with Vlad to reflect on his role in taking down the Cali Cartel and consulting on Netflix’s *Narcos* Season 3. Feistl discusses being portrayed by Michael Stahl-David, working with the show after the success of Javier Peña and Steve Murphy’s storylines, and what the series got right about Colombia’s drug war after Pablo Escobar.

The conversation expands into today’s cocaine trade, from increased coca production in Colombia to Mexico tunnels, corruption, money laundering, arms trafficking, and the challenges facing U.S. law enforcement. Feistl explains why, even with unlimited DEA resources, stopping cocaine from entering America may be impossible.

He also weighs in on marijuana legalization, the debate over legalizing cocaine, crack cocaine concerns, and the ongoing public health and crime impacts. Feistl closes by discussing his book *After Escobar*, co-written with Dave Mitchell and Jessica Boni.

In this VladTV interview, Jimmy DiModica details how labor union corruption allegedly operated on construction sites tied to New York and New Jersey organized crime. DiModica describes charging extra money for union books, lunch trucks, debris containers, and concrete deliveries, while explaining how pressure inside the union led to a leadership change during an emergency executive board meeting. He also recounts violent confrontations with contractors who, he says, agreed to pay but later used extra workers without providing the expected envelope, including an incident near Penn Station involving a Port Authority meeting, a slapjack, and rebar.  

DiModica connects the fallout to police building a case that eventually included RICO conspiracy, labor racketeering, extortion, and organized crime allegations. He also discusses his father’s position as a made man with the Gambino crime family and how that status affected influence across New York and New Jersey.

In this VladTV interview, John Franzese Jr. addresses rumors that he earned $500,000 for cooperating with the FBI, saying the real payments were far smaller and often tied to expenses, witness protection, and an undercover cover story involving steroids. Franzese details how cash was used during the investigation, what he received after entering the witness program, and why the public perception of “snitch money” doesn’t match his experience.

He also discusses the continuing danger after testifying and wearing wiretaps connected to Mafia figures, explaining why law enforcement still warns him to be careful in New York neighborhoods like Maspeth. Now living openly in Indianapolis, Franzese reflects on threats from organized crime, the realities of being labeled an informant, and why former cooperators may still face risks from the mob and other criminal groups. Watch for a candid look at FBI cooperation, witness protection, and life after the Mafia.

He explains his version of the gas station encounter where Spence allegedly sped off and crashed his Ferrari near the Dallas County Jail, while Mo3 continued home. Rainwater also details the January 2020 incident outside V Live nightclub, claiming he was jumped, injured, and robbed of his watch, leading to a civil lawsuit against Yella Beezy.

Rainwater says Mo3’s reaction was blunt—telling him to “go get your money”—and recalls earlier conflict with Yella Beezy dating back to a 2014 Kevin Gates concert in Dallas. He also discusses courtroom footage, the failed settlement offer, and a jury award he says totaled $375,000, with efforts underway to collect royalties.

--------
Former DEA agent Chris Feistl details his 12-plus years in Colombia across three tours, from the fall of the Cali Cartel to investigations targeting the North Valley Cartel, AUC paramilitaries, FARC, ELN, and other armed groups. Speaking with Vlad, Feistl explains how Colombian traffickers shifted cocaine routes through Mexico, believing they could avoid U.S. extradition—only to face American conspiracy indictments as drugs continued reaching the United States.  

The conversation covers the violent North Valley power struggle after Orlando Henao, including Diego Montoya “Don Diego” and Wilber Varela “Jabón,” whose war left thousands dead. Feistl also discusses the FBI’s role, Colombian security forces, Venezuela as a refuge for traffickers, and the endless cycle of cartel leadership replacements. He closes by reflecting on retiring from the DEA in 2014 and moving into private-sector anti-money laundering work.
